River Towns Bet on Floodplain Buyouts

By Mara Ostby · August 3, 2026

Three river towns in the fictional Carrow Valley voted this summer to buy out more than two hundred homes on the floodplain, the largest coordinated buyout the region has attempted. Officials said the program would turn the cleared land into wetlands and parks that can hold water during the spring floods that have damaged the same streets four times in a decade.

The buyouts are voluntary. Homeowners who accept receive the pre-flood market value of their property, paid from a mix of state disaster funds and a regional bond approved by voters last year. So far about sixty percent of eligible households have signed letters of intent, according to the valley's planning office.

Supporters argue that buyouts are cheaper over time than rebuilding. A study commissioned by the valley estimated that each dollar spent on buyouts would avoid roughly three dollars in future repair and emergency costs, although the authors cautioned that the estimate depends heavily on how often large floods occur in the coming decades.

Critics worry about what happens to the towns themselves. Removing whole blocks shrinks the tax base, and some residents fear that the neighborhoods left behind will lose the shops and schools that made them worth staying in. Several council members asked the state to guarantee replacement housing on higher ground before more families leave.

The planning office said construction of the first wetland areas could begin next spring. Residents who have not yet decided have until the end of the year to apply, and the office will hold public meetings in each town during the autumn to answer questions about appraisals and relocation help.
